summary: The lecture covers four major racial classifications (Negroid, Australoid, Caucasoid, Mongoloid) with physical features and geographic distribution; UNESCO's six language endangerment levels; Indian linguistic diversity including census data (1961: 187, 2001: 122 major languages), 8th Schedule evolution from 14 to 22 languages via constitutional amendments; major Indian language families (Dravidian, Austro-Asiatic, Sino-Tibetan, Indo-Aryan); and dialect types (geographical and social).
points: Four major racial groups: Negroid (Sub-Saharan Africa), Australoid (original Australians), Caucasoid (Europe/Middle East), Mongoloid (East Asia/Arctic) based on biological traits.
Negroid features: dark skin (high melanin), thick lips, wide nose, sloping forehead, long head; concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa.
Australoid features: dark brown skin, curly hair, prominent eye ridges, short stature; original Australians, not current European-descended population.
Caucasoid features: fair skin, wavy hair, sharp/narrow nose, vertical forehead; distributed across Europe, Middle East, North Africa.
Mongoloid features: yellowish/light brown skin, epicanthic fold (slanted eyes), prominent cheekbones, flat face, straight hair; found in East Asia and Arctic regions.
UNESCO language risk levels: Safe, Vulnerable, Definitely Endangered, Severely Endangered, Critically Endangered, Extinct.
India's 1961 Census recorded 187 major languages; 2001 Census recorded 122; 22 Eighth Schedule languages cover 97% of population.
Eighth Schedule originally had 14 languages (1950); Sindhi added by 21st Amendment (1967); Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali by 71st Amendment (1992); Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santali by 92nd Amendment (2003).
Major Indian language families: Dravidian (Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam, Kannada, Tulu), Austro-Asiatic (Munda), Sino-Tibetan (Assamese, Bodo, Manipuri), Indo-Aryan (Hindi, Urdu, Sanskrit).
Dialects: Geographical (region-based variation) and Social (community-based variation); mutually intelligible distinct forms of a language.
